messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 75
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: QA Engineer
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 46

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Smoke): Smoke or fire smell, Visual (Fire/Flames): Fire or flames, Weather Similarity: Similar weather conditions to when the event happened
  Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what I have done wrong, Rumination: Prevention: ruminate about how event could have been prevented, Thought Suppression: I try to push them out of my mind
  Threat: Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Carlos, a 75-year-old Latin American man who had spent decades working as a quality assurance engineer, had always prided himself on his ability to anticipate problems. His mind worked in systems, tracing every variable, every point of failure before it could occur. That was why, when the wildfire swept through his neighborhood three years ago, the memory had lodged itself in him not as a single event but as a permanent, repeating loop of what he should have done differently. He had smelled the smoke first, a sharp, acrid sweetness that seemed to seep through the cracks in the windows, and he had watched the orange glow crest the ridge with a sense of disbelief that hardened into horror. He and his wife had evacuated with only minutes to spare, but in the months and years that followed, Carlos could not stop returning to that moment. He would lie awake replaying the sequence: the way he had hesitated, the time he had wasted checking the gutters, the fact that he had not packed the photo albums. He told himself that if he had just been faster, smarter, more vigilant, the terror would not have taken root so deeply. He ruminated endlessly on how the event could have been prevented—if only he had cleared the brush earlier, if only he had installed a better sprinkler system, if only he had been a different kind of man.

The world after the fire became a landscape of hidden dangers. Carlos found himself scanning every room he entered for signs of smoke, his nostrils flaring involuntarily at the faintest whiff of a charred meal or a neighbor’s barbecue. The smell of smoke, even from a distant fireplace, sent his heart hammering against his ribs, his palms slick with sweat, his breath turning shallow and ragged. He became acutely aware of his own body’s betrayals: the way his hands trembled when he saw a flame on a stove, the way his legs felt weak and unsteady when the weather turned hot and dry, the wind picking up in that particular way that reminded him of that afternoon. He had come to believe that his physical reactions were a sign that something was fundamentally wrong with him, that his body was telling him the danger was still present, even when his rational mind knew otherwise. He was constantly on guard, watching for the first flicker of orange, listening for the crackle of burning wood. The startle response that seized him when a car backfired or a door slammed left him feeling humiliated and exposed, as if everyone could see how broken his internal alarm system had become.

His job, once a source of satisfaction, became a minefield. As a QA engineer, Carlos worked in an open-plan office where the break room was equipped with a microwave that occasionally burned popcorn. The smell would drift across his desk, and he would freeze, his eyes darting toward the ceiling vents, his mind instantly transported back to the night he had stood on the curb, watching his house disappear behind a wall of flame. He began to take his lunch in his car, eating quickly with the windows up, just to avoid the possibility of that smell. He tried to push the memories out of his mind, telling himself sternly to focus on the code in front of him, but the more he suppressed the images, the more they seemed to ambush him at unexpected moments. His concentration fractured; he made small errors in his work, errors that his younger colleagues caught before he did, and the shame of it only deepened his conviction that he was failing at the one thing he had always done well.

The consequences of his vigilance spread into his marriage. He insisted on checking the smoke detectors three times a day, and he would not allow his wife to light candles or use the fireplace, even on the coldest winter nights. She had grown quiet and patient, but Carlos could see the distance in her eyes, the way she no longer asked him why he was standing at the window, staring at the sky. He knew he was exhausting her, but he could not stop. What frightened him most was the thought that if another fire came, he would freeze again, that all his rumination and vigilance would amount to nothing, and that he would fail the one person he had spent his life trying to protect. It was that fear, finally, that brought him to a therapist’s office, not because he believed he could change, but because he was desperate for his wife to see him try.
